newsitem.title: USA: GM to be sole auto sponsor for Olympics -- sources.
newsitem.headline: GM to be sole auto sponsor for Olympics -- sources.

text.p: General Motors Corp will be the sole automotive sponsor for the U.S. Olympic Committee through the year 2008, according to sources close to GM and industry sources.
"GM will be the exclusive automotive sponsor for the U.S. Olympics through 2008, and is the official sponsor of the 2002 winter games in Salt Lake City," said a source close to GM.
GM, NBC, and the USOC have all declined to comment, although a news conference was scheduled for Wednesday.
Terms of the deal were not immediately known, although the Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that GM had committed to spending a total of $1 billion for the Olympics through 2008.

In an agreement with the USOC and General Electric Co's NBC Inc unit, GM would spend about $700 million for sponsorship-rights fees and television advertising, the Journal reported. Another $300 million would be spent on Olympics-related marketing, the paper reported.
GM's agreement would represent the largest sports sponsorship to date, according to the paper.
Lucent Technologies Inc, Xerox Corp, and UAL Corp all said on Tuesday they were in discussions with the USOC about being sponsors.
A Home Depot Inc spokesman said it was considering a sponsorship.
Anheuser-Busch Cos Inc was near an agreement to be the official beer sponsor, according to the Wall Street Journal. A company spokesman was not immediately available.
NBC has broadcast rights to the Olympics, beginning with the 2000 Summer Olympics in Sydney, Australia, through 2008.
The GM deal would be the first under a new approach, with the USOC and NBC working jointly to enlist corporations for both Olympic sponsorship and TV advertising.

One advertising source said that it was realistic for GM to spend $700 million for sponsorship and TV advertising alone. "It's a nice round number for domestic auto exclusivity for five Olympics," said the source.
The 2002 Winter Games in Salt Lake City is considered the "crown jewel," and is considered a more expensive advertising vehicle, advertising experts said.
